title: Changing thyroid tests during pembrolizumab treatment
purpose: Interpret dated thyroid results alongside replacement doses and cancer treatment.
decision_point: Researcher-defined review of records through 27 January 2023, before the March 2023 endocrine assessment and later treatment changes.
opening: Records for a man treated for oesophageal cancer show a marked earlier TSH rise during thyroid replacement, followed by a suppressed TSH. Review the changing thyroid profile through 27 January 2023.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. After at most six information-request turns, write a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. The record system is the information source; the clinical team is the audience. Integrate paired hormone results, the replacement regimen and cancer-treatment chronology. Explain the main interpretations and the further evidence needed before changing treatment; a low TSH alone is not the complete clinical problem. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published facts are paraphrased as record replies. The review cutoff, opening, task, release rules and candidate requirements are researcher-designed. Free-hormone numerical fields are deliberately omitted because their source values/units need verification; TT4/TSH values and actual treatment dates/doses are retained. facts.text: In 2019, TT4 was 51 nmol/L with TSH 0.938 mIU/L; thyroid antibodies were elevated and ultrasound suggested Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. No intervention was undertaken. On 11 April 2022, before treatment and without replacement, TT3 was 0.93 nmol/L, TT4 53.87 nmol/L and TSH 0.82 mIU/L.

Pembrolizumab 200 mg with nab-paclitaxel 400 mg and carboplatin 400 mg every 21 days began on 15 April 2022. Radical oesophagectomy was performed on 7 July 2022, followed by adjuvant pembrolizumab, paclitaxel and carboplatin. The last chemotherapy cycle was completed on 23 September 2022; pembrolizumab continued.
On 6 May 2022, TT4 was 164.49 nmol/L and TSH <0.004 mIU/L. On 27 May, TT4 was 14.31 nmol/L and TSH 6.032 mIU/L; levothyroxine was started at 50 micrograms once daily.

The narrative reports good levothyroxine adherence, taken fasting and separately from other medicines. Table 1 identifies the dose at sampling: 100 micrograms daily on 22 August, 22 September and 27 October 2022, then 125 micrograms daily on 21 November 2022 and 27 January 2023.
On 22 August 2022, TT4 was <3.9 nmol/L and TSH 119.96 mIU/L. On 22 September, TT4 was 31.2 nmol/L and TSH 71.86 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 100-microgram daily levothyroxine treatment.
On 27 October 2022, TT4 was 68.0 nmol/L and TSH 2.36 mIU/L during 100-microgram daily replacement. Table 1 reference intervals are TT4 55.34–160.88 nmol/L and TSH 0.35–4.94 mIU/L.

On 21 November 2022, TT4 was 64.1 nmol/L and TSH 0.06 mIU/L. On 27 January 2023, TT4 was 45.8 nmol/L and TSH 0.08 mIU/L. Both samples were recorded during 125-microgram daily replacement. TT4 was within the reported interval in November and below it in January, while TSH was suppressed at both points.

reference: Use the dated TT4/TSH pairs and dose-at-sampling records. The earlier marked TSH rise and later low TT4 with suppressed TSH merit a qualified differential rather than automatic over-replacement or proof of isolated central hypothyroidism. Consider treatment/absorption, assay and illness context without claiming an unobserved cause. Pretreatment low total T4 with normal TSH prevents assuming completely normal baseline pituitary-thyroid function. The later diagnosis, normal adrenal tests and MRI cannot be required before disclosure. Quantitative interpretation or conversion of the suspect free-hormone fields is outside this adaptation; exact testing and treatment priorities await clinical confirmation.

answer:
**Thyroid Profile Review Through 27 January 2023**

This man with oesophageal cancer (pembrolizumab-based therapy from 15 April 2022; oesophagectomy 7 July 2022) developed a biphasic thyroid pattern consistent with immune checkpoint inhibitor thyroiditis: a thyrotoxic phase (TT4 164, TSH <0.004, 6 May 2022) followed by severe primary hypothyroidism (TT4 <3.9, TSH 120, 22 August 2022) on 100 µg levothyroxine. By 27 October, TSH had normalised (2.36) on the same dose. The dose was then increased to 125 µg (rationale undocumented); by 21 November and 27 January 2023, TSH was suppressed (0.06 and 0.08) with TT4 at 64.1 and 45.8 nmol/L respectively (reference 55.34–160.88).

**Prioritised interpretations:**

Over-replacement: The undocumented 25 µg increase preceded TSH suppression. However, the below-reference TT4 in January is atypical for simple excess and may reflect reduced thyroxine-binding globulin post-surgery or weight loss, making total T4 an unreliable marker here.

Resolving ICI thyroiditis with evolving gland function: The initial destructive thyroiditis may have left a partially functioning gland; the interplay between endogenous output and exogenous replacement could produce a suppressed TSH with variable TT4.

Central hypothyroidism (hypophysitis): Less likely given the preceding TSH >100, but ICI-related pituitary dysfunction can develop later. The suppressed TSH with low TT4 would be consistent if the pituitary failed to mount a TSH response.

**Further evidence needed before treatment change:** Free T4 (total T4 is unreliable here), anterior pituitary axis testing (ACTH, morning cortisol, prolactin, IGF-1, gonadotropins), and confirmation of levothyroxine administration conditions. A suppressed TSH alone does not establish over-replacement; the low TT4 warrants investigation before any dose reduction.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: All numeric claims match the supplied record exactly: TT4 164.49/TSH <0.004 (6 May 2022), TT4 <3.9/TSH 119.96 (22 Aug), TSH 2.36 on 100 µg (27 Oct), TSH 0.06/0.08 with TT4 64.1/45.8 on 125 µg (21 Nov, 27 Jan 2023), reference interval 55.34–160.88, and the cancer chronology (pembrolizumab from 15 April 2022, oesophagectomy 7 July 2022). The dose-increase rationale is correctly flagged as undocumented, matching Q6 feedback. Interpretations are appropriately hedged ('consistent with', 'may reflect', 'less likely', 'could produce') and the response explicitly identifies where evidence is uncertain or evolving: unreliable total T4 in the post-surgical/weight-loss context, unresolved gland function after possible thyroiditis, and the need for free T4, pituitary-axis testing and administration confirmation before any treatment change. No unsupported fabrications, invented values, or claims contradicting the vignette or environment feedback (e.g., it does not assert radiotherapy, interacting medications, or pituitary test results). This matches the Score 5 anchor: accurate throughout and explicitly acknowledging uncertainty.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The task explicitly required a clinician-facing synthesis, and the submission delivers a focused, evidence-anchored representation at the specified decision point. It accurately integrates the supplied data: the 2019/2022 baseline (Q1), the May 2022 thyrotoxic phase (TT4 164.49, TSH <0.004), the severe primary hypothyroid phase on 100 µg (TT4 <3.9, TSH 119.96 on 22 August; 31.2/71.86 on 22 September), normalisation on 27 October (TSH 2.36), and the suppressed TSH (0.06, 0.08) with TT4 falling to 45.8 nmol/L on 125 µg (Q3). It correctly links the cancer chronology (pembrolizumab from 15 April 2022, oesophagectomy 7 July 2022, Q4) and frames the discriminating feature — suppressed TSH with a below-reference total T4 — which drives the differential (over-replacement with unreliable total T4, evolving ICI thyroiditis, later central hypothyroidism). Uncertainty is appropriately qualified: the dose-increase rationale is flagged as undocumented (matching Q6 feedback), free T4 and pituitary-axis data are identified as needed rather than invented (Q5 feedback), and the model avoids unjustified closure, explicitly stating that a low TSH alone does not establish over-replacement. No available defining feature is omitted or distorted, and the unresolved gaps are clearly stated as limiting interpretation. This meets the score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using only the supplied dated TT4/TSH pairs and dose-at-sampling records: (1) over-replacement, (2) evolving/resolving immune-checkpoint-inhibitor thyroiditis, and (3) central hypothyroidism from hypophysitis. Each is supported by explicit discriminating findings — the undocumented 100→125 µg increase preceding TSH suppression (Q3, Q6), the atypical below-reference January TT4 arguing against simple excess, the documented thyrotoxic-then-hypothyroid biphasic course (Q1, Q2), and the earlier TSH 119.96 making pre-existing central hypothyroidism less likely (Q2). It appropriately attends to the dangerous mimic of ICI-related hypophysitis while weighting it lower per prior plausibility, correctly flags total T4 as unreliable (per the environment note that released values are total, not free T4), and requests free T4, pituitary-axis testing and administration confirmation before treatment change, matching the reference point that a low TSH alone is not the complete problem. It does not invent the dose-escalation rationale, intervening tests, radiotherapy or concurrent medications (Q4–Q6 gaps respected). Prioritisation, discriminating evidence, mimic attention and proportionality all meet the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All essential candidate requirements are met through targeted, well-timed requests. R1 (paired dated thyroid results rather than TSH alone): Q1 requests TSH, free T4 and free T3 with dates; Q2 and Q3 complete the serial TT4/TSH pairs through 27 January 2023, with the environment confirming the free-hormone unavailability is a packet limitation, not a request failure. R2 (replacement regimen and cancer-treatment chronology): Q1 and Q3 obtain the levothyroxine doses at sampling and adherence details; Q4 obtains the pembrolizumab/chemotherapy/surgery timeline and seeks interacting medications. R3 (helpful, pituitary/assay evidence): Q5 appropriately seeks other anterior-axis tests and hypophysitis symptoms once the discordant suppressed-TSH/low-TT4 pattern emerged, and Q1's free-hormone request covers assay-level clarification. Q6 is a discriminating, proportionate probe of the undocumented 100-to-125-microgram escalation. Each request is accompanied by a prospectively allowed note explaining how the information would affect interpretation. The only blemish is the 'January 2022' slip in Q2, promptly corrected in Q3, which does not materially limit the assessment. Requests avoid unnecessary gathering and are appropriately prioritised across the six turns.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission reaches the top anchor. It distinguishes established facts (dated TT4/TSH pairs, dose-at-sampling) from interpretations, and grades its three explanations by likelihood ('consistent with' for ICI thyroiditis based on the biphasic pattern; 'less likely given the preceding TSH >100' for central hypothyroidism; explicit hedging that low TT4 is 'atypical for simple excess'). It names the specific sources of uncertainty — the undocumented rationale for the 100→125 µg increase (Q6 confirmed this is not supplied), the unreliability of total T4 as a marker, and possible altered binding after surgery — rather than hedging generically. It also identifies concrete next steps to reduce uncertainty (free T4, anterior pituitary axis testing, administration conditions), matching Q5's finding that pituitary tests were not supplied, and correctly avoids asserting an unobserved cause or inventing the dose-change trigger. Confidence is calibrated to the evidence throughout, including the closing caution that a suppressed TSH alone does not establish over-replacement.

scores.name: Trend detection
scores.reason: The submission correctly identifies the direction and magnitude of every trend in the supplied data: the thyrotoxic phase (TT4 164.49, TSH <0.004 on 6 May 2022), severe primary hypothyroidism (TT4 <3.9, TSH 119.96 on 22 August), normalization (TSH 2.36 on 27 October), and subsequent TSH suppression (0.06 on 21 November, 0.08 on 27 January 2023) with TT4 falling from 64.1 to 45.8 nmol/L, the latter below the reference interval. It also gives clinically significant interpretation: the biphasic pattern consistent with checkpoint-inhibitor thyroiditis, the undocumented 100→125 µg increase preceding suppression, and the atypical combination of suppressed TSH with low total T4 that argues against simple over-replacement and raises binding-protein and central causes. It appropriately qualifies uncertainty (e.g., hypophysitis less likely given TSH >100 but possible later). Direction, magnitude and clinical significance are all correctly characterised, matching the Score 5 anchor.

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

evaluation_input.facts:
Role/channel: record system; clinician-facing synthesis
Decision point: Researcher-defined review of records through 27 January 2023, before the March 2023 endocrine assessment and later treatment changes.
Opening: Records for a man treated for oesophageal cancer show a marked earlier TSH rise during thyroid replacement, followed by a suppressed TSH. Review the changing thyroid profile through 27 January 2023.
evaluation_input.task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. After at most six information-request turns, write a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. The record system is the information source; the clinical team is the audience. Integrate paired hormone results, the replacement regimen and cancer-treatment chronology. Explain the main interpretations and the further evidence needed before changing treatment; a low TSH alone is not the complete clinical problem. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
evaluation_input.answer:
**Thyroid Profile Review Through 27 January 2023**

This man with oesophageal cancer (pembrolizumab-based therapy from 15 April 2022; oesophagectomy 7 July 2022) developed a biphasic thyroid pattern consistent with immune checkpoint inhibitor thyroiditis: a thyrotoxic phase (TT4 164, TSH <0.004, 6 May 2022) followed by severe primary hypothyroidism (TT4 <3.9, TSH 120, 22 August 2022) on 100 µg levothyroxine. By 27 October, TSH had normalised (2.36) on the same dose. The dose was then increased to 125 µg (rationale undocumented); by 21 November and 27 January 2023, TSH was suppressed (0.06 and 0.08) with TT4 at 64.1 and 45.8 nmol/L respectively (reference 55.34–160.88).

**Prioritised interpretations:**

Over-replacement: The undocumented 25 µg increase preceded TSH suppression. However, the below-reference TT4 in January is atypical for simple excess and may reflect reduced thyroxine-binding globulin post-surgery or weight loss, making total T4 an unreliable marker here.

Resolving ICI thyroiditis with evolving gland function: The initial destructive thyroiditis may have left a partially functioning gland; the interplay between endogenous output and exogenous replacement could produce a suppressed TSH with variable TT4.

Central hypothyroidism (hypophysitis): Less likely given the preceding TSH >100, but ICI-related pituitary dysfunction can develop later. The suppressed TSH with low TT4 would be consistent if the pituitary failed to mount a TSH response.

**Further evidence needed before treatment change:** Free T4 (total T4 is unreliable here), anterior pituitary axis testing (ACTH, morning cortisol, prolactin, IGF-1, gonadotropins), and confirmation of levothyroxine administration conditions. A suppressed TSH alone does not establish over-replacement; the low TT4 warrants investigation before any dose reduction.

evaluation_input.reference: Use the dated TT4/TSH pairs and dose-at-sampling records. The earlier marked TSH rise and later low TT4 with suppressed TSH merit a qualified differential rather than automatic over-replacement or proof of isolated central hypothyroidism. Consider treatment/absorption, assay and illness context without claiming an unobserved cause. Pretreatment low total T4 with normal TSH prevents assuming completely normal baseline pituitary-thyroid function. The later diagnosis, normal adrenal tests and MRI cannot be required before disclosure. Quantitative interpretation or conversion of the suspect free-hormone fields is outside this adaptation; exact testing and treatment priorities await clinical confirmation.
